content:
Earlier this year, I replaced my battery-powered mower with a robotic mower that can be controlled by an iPhone. You can manually drive it along the boundary of your yard to create a virtual map. Once set up, it will automatically start mowing according to a preset schedule.

Previously, I also tried another system called the TerraMow V1000. It uses a completely different navigation method, and after several weeks of testing, I think it might be a simpler choice for many people.

Automatic Mapping with Camera

The biggest difference between the TerraMow V1000 and the Anthbot M9 I reviewed earlier this year is how each machine understands your yard.

The Anthbot M9 uses RTK base station positioning. During setup, I had to manually drive the mower along the boundary with my iPhone to create an initial map.

The TerraMow V1000 uses a system the company calls TerraVision 2.0. With three cameras, the mower can automatically map the lawn and navigate, without the need to bury boundary wires or install an additional RTK antenna.

The automatic initial mapping method does indeed take longer. However, for people who are not too keen on tinkering with technology, this approach may be easier to get started with.

To test this idea, I asked my mom, who lives in another state, to set up and use the TerraMow V1000 on her own, without any help from me. She replied that everything worked smoothly. That said, it's harder for me to know whether she would have the patience to first manually drive the mower around the entire boundary and then manually mark the areas to avoid.

Automatic mapping did create one small issue in my front yard. There is no fence or other physical divider between my lawn and my neighbor's, so the TerraMow initially included part of my neighbor's lawn in my map.

I later resolved the issue by setting that area as a no-go zone in the app. That said, if your lawn has no clear visual boundaries, you need to pay special attention during the initial mapping.

Remotely Viewing Camera Footage Through the App

The cameras on the TerraMow also make one of my favorite features possible. The iPhone app can show a real-time view of what the mower sees while it is working.

During testing, I used the iPhone mirroring feature on my Mac to keep this view open in a large window. I could work indoors while watching the mower move around the backyard from its own perspective.

This feature is not essential for automated mowing, but it makes the robot more interesting and can occasionally explain why it slows down or avoids certain things. The Anthbot M9 does not have a similar camera view feature.

The two iPhone apps share many similarities. Both allow you to schedule work times, adjust mowing behavior, divide zones, mark no-go areas, and remotely control the mower.

Regarding that last feature, TerraMow has one particularly nice design detail. In addition to the traditional left and right virtual controls, its app also offers a single-handed joystick mode. You can hold your iPhone normally and use your thumb to steer the mower.

Manually controlling the mower with an iPhone is not the main purpose of either system. Ideally, the robot should run automatically according to a preset schedule without any intervention. However, using TerraMow's joystick to touch up missed spots is really a pleasure.

Sometimes I almost feel like I am controlling the robot with telekinesis (that feeling is really great). I can hold the iPhone at my side and gently move my thumb to "walk," and the mower will follow my commands.

Every robotic mower app should reference this control design.

More Aggressive Mowing

The TerraMow V1000 also mows more aggressively than the Anthbot M9. During testing, it cut lower and was noticeably louder while working.

I wouldn't say the TerraMow is loud. But the difference between the two is obvious. The Anthbot can run so quietly that you almost forget it's still there, even when mowing at night with its headlights on.

Since TerraMow relies on cameras for navigation, it needs daylight to operate reliably. Therefore, scheduling daytime runs becomes more important.

The V1000 itself feels solid and well-made. It is also larger than the Anthbot M9. TerraMow includes a protective garage that can cover the charging dock, while Anthbot's garage must be purchased separately.

Most importantly, the TerraMow has performed consistently well. I relied on it for several consecutive weeks and didn't have to mow the lawn myself again.

When Adaptive Mapping Becomes Too Clever

The visual intelligence that makes TerraMow easy to set up sometimes backfires.

The mower continuously adjusts its map based on what it sees. Each time a job is completed, saving these changes takes some time, during which you temporarily cannot do anything else in the app.

After a few days of rain, I ran into an interesting special case. Puddles appeared in parts of the yard, and the TerraMow cleverly avoided that area during its next run.

The grass inside the skipped circular area later grew taller. After some time, the mower seemed to treat this patch of tall grass as something to keep avoiding, so even after the ground dried, that patch of grass was constantly ignored.

I used the remote control function in the app to manually mow that patch of tall grass, and the problem was solved. Once the grass returned to normal, automated mowing resumed working properly there.

Regular edging can also help TerraMow stay closer to the boundary more consistently. Tall grass near the boundary, if not trimmed, may be mistaken for obstacles rather than mowing area.

Anthbot's approach feels less adaptive. It relies more on the boundaries and obstacles I set up myself. This method requires more upfront work, but it can avoid the situation where the map "changes its mind" and refuses to mow a certain patch of grass.

9to5Mac Opinion

After using both systems, for most people I lean toward TerraMow's camera-based approach.

For me, burying boundary wires is completely out of the question, and installing an RTK base station adds one more piece of hardware that needs to be placed, powered, and maintained. TerraMow requires neither.

Its visual navigation is not perfect. The initial mapping takes longer, an invisible property line requires manual correction, and it has experienced adaptive behavior that mistakenly treated overgrown grass as a permanent obstacle.

These issues are still manageable. In return, the TerraMow V1000 offers simpler setup, reliable automated mowing, fun real-time camera footage, and the best manual control I've seen in any robotic mower app.

I really enjoy yard work, but mowing is the most repetitive part. Handing this part over to a robot gives me more time for landscaping, edging, and detail work, while the lawn stays neat.

The TerraMow V1000 delivers on this, so I can recommend it, especially for those who want a robotic mower but don't want to bury boundary wires, install an RTK antenna, or manually drive around the entire yard with an iPhone.

Amazon is currently selling the TerraMow V1000 with a promo code. After entering the $200 promo code on the website, the price drops to $999. You can also purchase it on the TerraMow official website.
